about.description: A local tool for IP reputation analysis, URL scanning, DMARC reports, e-mail source analysis and preparing AbuseIPDB abuse reports.

about.limits_hint:
Limits of the free plans.
VirusTotal, urlscan and OpenRouter report the real limits and the LLM credit when you click "Refresh limits" (one request to each service; these requests do not use up quota).
AbuseIPDB and Cloudflare take the values from the rate-limit headers of the latest requests.
GreyNoise and OTX report nothing, so Seisa counts its own requests.
When a service answers with error 429 (limit exceeded), its row gets a "limit exceeded" badge and a full counter until the next successful answer.
Assumed limits: AbuseIPDB 5,000/day | GreyNoise 50/week | OTX 10,000/hour | Cloudflare 1,200/5 minutes.

lookup.subtitle:
Check the reputation of an IP address or a domain in several independent threat-intelligence sources at once and see one aggregate risk score.
For an IP address: VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, Cloudflare Radar, AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise and WHOIS/rDNS.
For a domain: VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, Cloudflare Radar, WHOIS/DNS, local heuristics.

dmarc.subtitle: Upload aggregate DMARC reports from mail providers to see which servers send messages on behalf of your domain, whether they pass SPF/DKIM and their alignment, and which IP addresses look suspicious.
dmarc.drop_multiple: You can upload several reports at once; .xml, .gz and .zip files are accepted
dmarc.no_auth_data: no auth_results/{section} data in this record
dmarc.no_records: No records to display in the selected files.
dmarc.banner_bad_one: {n} source fails both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_other: {n} sources fail both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_hint: Check whether these are legitimate senders missing from your SPF/DKIM setup or someone spoofing your domain.
dmarc.banner_warn_one: {n} source fails SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_warn_other: {n} sources fail SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_good: All sources pass both SPF and DKIM.
dmarc.known_sender: Probably a known sender: {name} (the rDNS name is confirmed by a forward DNS lookup).
dmarc.known_sender_fix: If this is your service, fix its SPF/DKIM setup instead of blocking the address.
dmarc.h_fix: What to fix if this is a legitimate sender
dmarc.fix_dkim_missing: DKIM: the report has no signature. Enable DKIM signing with a key of your domain at this sender.
dmarc.fix_dkim_fail: DKIM: the signature of {domain} (selector {selector}) failed verification. Check that the public key in DNS ({selector}._domainkey.{domain}) is current.
dmarc.fix_dkim_misaligned: DKIM: the signature passes, but for {domain}, which differs from the From header domain ({from}), so it is not aligned. Make the sender sign with your own domain.
dmarc.fix_spf_missing: SPF: the report has no result. Check that the envelope (Return-Path) domain has an SPF record.
dmarc.fix_spf_fail: SPF: the address {ip} is not allowed by the SPF record of {domain}. If this is a legitimate sender, add it to the record (preferably through the service's include:).
dmarc.fix_spf_misaligned: SPF: passes for {domain}, which differs from the From header domain ({from}), so it is not aligned. Make the sender use your own domain as Return-Path or rely on DKIM.
dmarc.timeline_legend: A bar is the number of messages that day (tallest: {max}); the red part is the messages that failed DMARC.
dmarc.legend_spf: Checks whether the sending server's IP address is authorised in the SPF record of the envelope-from (Return-Path) domain. auth_results is the raw result (pass, fail, softfail, neutral, none, temperror, permerror) with the domain and scope (mfrom or helo); policy_evaluated says whether it also matched the From domain (alignment) and so counts for DMARC.
dmarc.legend_dkim: Checks the cryptographic signature the sending server added to the message (the d= domain and the s= selector). auth_results is the raw signature result; policy_evaluated says whether the signing domain matched the From domain and so counts for DMARC.
dmarc.legend_policy: p is what receivers should do with mail that fails DMARC: none (only report), quarantine (spam folder), reject (refuse). sp is the same for subdomains, pct the share of messages the policy applies to, adkim/aspf the alignment (relaxed allows subdomains, strict needs an exact match), fo the failure-report options, np the policy for non-existent subdomains. Decision is what the receiver actually did and can differ from p because of an override. A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and is aligned.
dmarc.err_no_unpack: this browser cannot unpack archives - unpack the file and load the .xml
dmarc.err_too_large: the unpacked report is too large
dmarc.err_archive: the archive could not be read
dmarc.hint_none_ready: {domain}: p=none only monitors, and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to quarantine, then reject.
dmarc.hint_none_risky: {domain}: p=none only monitors, so messages from suspicious sources are delivered untouched. Fix legitimate senders first, then tighten the policy.
dmarc.hint_quarantine_ready: {domain}: p=quarantine and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to reject.
dmarc.hint_pct: {domain}: pct={pct} - the policy applies to only {pct}% of failing messages, the rest is handled with a milder action.
dmarc.legend_table: The SPF and DKIM counts in the sources table are the policy_evaluated results (after alignment), not the raw auth_results. A source can therefore show SPF as failed although auth_results says pass for another domain - typical for forwarded mail, which receivers often mark with an override such as forwarded or mailing_list.
dmarc.legend_risk: HIGH: the source fails both SPF and DKIM (not aligned), so DMARC fails. MEDIUM: only one of the two methods fails, so DMARC can still pass through the other. LOW: SPF and DKIM both pass. The rating is per IP address and covers all its messages; it does not say whether the sender is legitimate, only whether its mail is authenticated correctly.
dmarc.legend_tiles: Suspicious are the sources with high or medium risk. DMARC pass rate is the share of messages in which SPF or DKIM passed with alignment. Policy decisions are the numbers of messages the receiver rejected (reject), quarantined (quarantine) or delivered untouched (none); with p=none even failing mail is delivered, so none does not mean the message was fine. An override (e.g. forwarded, mailing_list, local_policy) is the reason the receiver departed from the policy.
dmarc.legend_geo: The geo button asks for the registration of the address block (RDAP: country, owner, network name) and for the reverse DNS (rDNS) name of the address. A known sender (e.g. Google, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES) is named only when the rDNS name resolves back to the same address, because the PTR record is set by the owner of the IP block and can be forged. No label does not mean the source is bad.
dmarc.legend_fix: The list in an expanded source comes from its records: no DKIM signature, a DKIM key that fails verification, a signature or SPF pass for a different domain than the From header (no alignment), or an address missing from the SPF record. It applies only to a legitimate sender; if you do not recognise the source, fix nothing and consider reporting the abuse instead.
dmarc.legend_compare: The comparison sets this import against the previous import of the same domain saved in History: new sources, sources that are gone, sources with worse risk and the DMARC pass rate. The chart shows the number of messages per day (by the start of the report period, in UTC), and the red part is the messages that failed DMARC.

em.prep_notes: Preparing the source for the model: {notes}.
em.no_key: No OpenRouter key (OPENROUTER_API_KEY in .env) - showing the deterministic analysis only.
em.model_writing: The model is writing the analysis...

em.citations_bad: Citation check: {bad} of {n} checked items do not match the source.
em.citations_hint: This is not always an error (it may be an example, a paraphrase or an abbreviation), but check these places before treating them as true:
em.truncated_banner: The analysis was cut off by the response length limit - its final parts are missing.
em.f.title: Deterministic analysis
em.f.md_intro: Computed locally by Seisa, without a language model. URLs are defanged.
em.f.no_flags: No anomalies were detected automatically (that does not mean there are none).
em.f.received: Message route: Received headers ({n}), from the top (newest)
em.f.received_help: Trust boundary: only the Received header added by the recipient's server is reliable. The roles below are a code heuristic; the final assessment is made by the analysis.
em.f.auth_count: Authentication: SPF / DKIM / DMARC / ARC ({n} result headers)
em.f.auth_help: Only the Authentication-Results written by the recipient's server (authserv-id) counts. A result written by anyone else is just their claim.
em.f.filters: Recipient's anti-spam filters and flags set by the sender
em.f.filters_help: The filter headers were written by the recipient's server (they carry evidential weight). The sender's flags are its own claims - not proof, only an element of pressure or tracking.
em.f.opaque: Headers unreadable for humans (internal Microsoft blobs)
em.f.epochs: Epoch timestamps found in the headers
em.f.html: HTML content: links, remote elements, hidden content
em.f.wrapped_anchor: Large part of the content wrapped in a single link
em.f.dup_headers: Repeated headers that should appear only once
em.f.casing: Different letter case in header names (trace of different programs)
em.f.intro: Computed locally by Seisa, without a language model: these are hard facts extracted from the source. The model receives them as input.
em.x.title: E-mail analysis: {subject}
em.x.truncated: Note: the LLM analysis was cut off by the length limit (the final parts are missing).
em.x.citations_ok: Checked {n} items (IP addresses, quoted headers, SCL/BCL values, identifiers): all match the source.
em.x.citations_bad: {bad} of {n} checked items do not match the source (not always an error: an example, a paraphrase, an abbreviation):
em.saved_empty: No saved analyses. Every completed analysis is saved together with the raw e-mail in the data/analyses directory.
em.dup_other_lang: That analysis is in a different language than the interface; a new analysis in {ui} is paid (a cost similar to the previous one).
em.lang_notice: This LLM analysis was written in {lang}, while the interface is in {ui}. The text of the analysis and the facts stay in the language they were created in (the interface labels are in {ui}).
em.gl.spf: Sender Policy Framework: the domain of the envelope sender (MAIL FROM) lists which servers may send its mail; the receiver checks the IP of the connecting server against that list.
em.gl.dkim: DomainKeys Identified Mail: the sending domain signs chosen headers and the body; the receiver verifies the signature with the public key published in DNS.
em.gl.dmarc: The policy of the From domain: SPF or DKIM must pass AND align with the From domain; p= says what to do otherwise (none, quarantine, reject).
em.gl.arc: Authenticated Received Chain: intermediaries (forwarders, mailing lists) seal the authentication results they saw, so the final receiver can still trust them after SPF/DKIM broke on the way.
em.gl.mta: Mail Transfer Agent: a server program that passes mail between servers over SMTP (Postfix, Exim, Exchange).
em.gl.mua: Mail User Agent: the mail client of a person (Thunderbird, Outlook, a phone app).
em.gl.mda: Mail Delivery Agent: the last program on the route, which puts the message into the recipient's mailbox.
em.gl.esmtp: Extended SMTP: SMTP with extensions such as STARTTLS or authentication; it appears in the "with" field of Received.
em.gl.lmtp: Local Mail Transfer Protocol: hand-over of a message between a mail server and the mailbox store on the operator's side.
em.gl.helo: The name a connecting server announces about itself in SMTP (HELO/EHLO). It is only a declaration and can say anything.
em.gl.ptr: Reverse DNS record of an IP address: the name the owner of the IP assigned to it. The IP owner sets it, so it is a hint, not proof.
em.gl.rdns: Reverse DNS: the name a given IP address resolves to (the PTR record).
em.gl.fcrdns: Forward-confirmed reverse DNS: the PTR name resolves back to the same IP; only then reverse DNS carries any weight.
em.gl.tls: Transport Layer Security: encrypts a single SMTP hop only (not end to end) and says nothing about whether the sender is legitimate.
em.gl.mime: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions: how a message is divided into parts (text, HTML, attachments) and encoded.
em.gl.scl: Spam Confidence Level (Microsoft): 0-1 clean, 5-6 spam, 9 the highest confidence of spam.
em.gl.bcl: Bulk Complaint Level (Microsoft): how many complaints a bulk sender attracts, 0-9.
em.gl.authserv: The name of the server that wrote an Authentication-Results header. Only the header written by the recipient's own server can be trusted.
em.gl.returnpath: The envelope sender (MAIL FROM) recorded by the recipient's server; bounces go there. It can differ from From:.
em.gl.replyto: The address replies go to. It is not signed by default and phishing often points it at the attacker.
em.gl.messageid: A unique identifier assigned by the sending system; its domain often reveals the real software or host.
em.gl.received: A header each server adds at the top when it accepts the message: read it from the bottom (start of the route) to the top (recipient).
em.gl.envelope: The envelope (MAIL FROM / RCPT TO) is what SMTP delivers by; the letter (From, To, Subject) is what the reader sees. They need not match.

lookup.agreement_title.single: Only one source reports this field, so there is nothing to compare.
lookup.agreement_title.agree: All sources that report this field give the same value.
lookup.agreement_title.majority: The sources disagree; the value shown is the one most of them report. Click for the other values.
lookup.agreement_title.conflict: The sources disagree and none has a majority; the value shown comes from the highest-priority source (the registry, RDAP, first). Click for all values.
lookup.raw_summary: Stored summary (the raw response is not kept in history)
lookup.nothing_more: Nothing more to show here; see the full API response.
lookup.f.name: Name
lookup.identity_pointer: What this source reports about the owner, registration, network and DNS is listed first (the identity section merges it with the other sources).
lookup.compare_trend: Score of the last {n} scans (the outlined bar is this one)
lookup.bt_title: Batch summary - {n} indicators, highest score first
lookup.legend.score: One number 0-100 combined from the sources that voted (noisy-OR model): agreeing sources reinforce each other, a strong signal is not averaged away and a source without data does not vote. Below {medium} is low, from {medium} to below {high} is medium, {high} and above is high. A known good IP (AbuseIPDB whitelist, GreyNoise benign/RIOT, OTX validation) is capped at {cap} unless another source has a strong contradicting signal. For a domain the voters are VirusTotal, OTX and the local heuristics (AbuseIPDB and GreyNoise only know IP addresses).
lookup.legend.risk: How dangerous one source considers the address or domain, 0-100, on a scale chosen for what that service measures. Credibility is the largest share of that vote that counts, because the sources are not fully independent (VirusTotal absorbs part of the same reports as AbuseIPDB).
lookup.legend.signal: A source with a source risk of {medium} or more (Medium or High) counts as a signal: its card opens automatically and its jump link is amber. Other cards stay closed but hold the same details. Sources that gave no answer (error, no key, limit reached, not applicable) share one bar at the end of the list.
lookup.legend.identity: For an IP address: ASN, owner, country and network. For a domain: registrar, dates, name servers, IP addresses, mail records, category and popularity. Merged from every source that reports them, after normalising the values. Badges: ✓ all sources agree, ≈ a majority agrees (click for the other values), ⚠ no majority, 1 source means there is nothing to compare. The card is collapsed while the sources agree and opens by itself when they do not.
lookup.legend.priority: On a tie the value of the highest-priority source is shown: RDAP (the registry itself) first for owner, network and contact, VirusTotal first for ASN, DNS before WHOIS for name servers. The priority never overrides a majority, and the identity never changes the score.
lookup.legend.country: The registration country (RDAP: where the address block was registered) and the geolocation country (where the address appears to be) are separate fields. They often differ for hosting, anycast and leased ranges, which is normal.
lookup.legend.confidence: AbuseIPDB: how sure it is that the address is abusive, based on the reports of the last 90 days weighted by the trust in the reporters. It is not a count of reports.
lookup.legend.greynoise: GreyNoise: malicious = seen attacking, benign = a known harmless scanner or service, unknown = seen but not classified. Noise means mass internet scanning, not necessarily an attack aimed at you.
lookup.legend.riot: GreyNoise list of common business services (CDNs, clouds, search engines). An address on it is expected to look noisy and is treated as known good.
lookup.legend.pulses: AlienVault OTX: community threat reports that mention the address. Fresh, enriched pulses (adversary, malware family, ATT&CK) count more than old bulk lists, and OTX alone never gives a high score.
lookup.legend.whitelisted: AbuseIPDB: the address is on its allow list (known good), so its source risk is 0.
lookup.legend.domain: WHOIS gives the registration (registrar, creation and expiry date, status); DNS gives what the domain points to (A/AAAA addresses, name servers, MX, SPF, DMARC, CAA). Wildcard DNS means any subdomain resolves. A dangling NS is a delegation to a name server that does not exist, which lets whoever registers that name take the zone over. Popularity is the Cloudflare Radar ranking: an exact rank only for the top 100, otherwise a bucket (top 200, 500 ...).
lookup.legend.heuristics: Domains only, computed on your machine from the name and the WHOIS age: registered less than 90 days ago, look-alike characters from mixed alphabets, punycode, a frequently abused TLD, a random-looking label, lure words (login, secure ...). Weak hints with a credibility of 0.4, so they can lift a domain to medium but never to high on their own.
lookup.legend.comparison: Shown when the same indicator is in the History: the previous score, the difference, the sources whose risk moved by 10 or more, and one bar per earlier scan (the outlined one is the current scan). The History keeps 25 unpinned entries.
rb.payload_title: What will be sent to the API
rb.payload_hint: Exactly what the backend sends to AbuseIPDB: the comment after cleaning (ASCII only, at most 1024 characters), the categories without duplicates and the time in UTC.
rb.hop_internal: An intermediate hop - usually the recipient's or the provider's own infrastructure, not the sender.
rb.check.pii_scan: No personal data in the comment (scan)
rb.hint.combine: {name} is meant to accompany a more specific category - add the one that describes the actual attack.
rb.hint.vpn: {name} is a combined category for addresses of VPN services - use it together with the category of the actual abuse.
rb.hint.iot: {name}: name the type of the targeted device in the comment.
rb.hint.spoofing: {name}: the sender passed authentication (SPF or DMARC pass), so the headers do not confirm spoofing.
rb.ip_whitelisted: This address is on the AbuseIPDB whitelist - a report is unlikely to have any effect.
rb.ip_redundant: In the last {days} days this address already has reports in one of the chosen categories (count: {n}) - a new one probably adds only noise. Report it only if you have new facts.
rb.pii_title: The comment may contain personal data
rb.pii_hint: AbuseIPDB shows comments publicly and is not responsible for personal data you reveal - check whether it is your data and mask or remove it before sending.
rb.pii_confirm: The comment still contains {n} item(s) that look like personal data. Send anyway?
rb.sent_score: AbuseIPDB now rates this address at {score}%.
rb.another_ip: Report another address from this e-mail:
rb.md.title: AbuseIPDB report: {ip}
rb.cat.1: Tampering with DNS records so that traffic is redirected.
rb.cat.2: Forged data planted in a DNS server's cache.
rb.cat.4: Taking part in a distributed denial-of-service attack.
rb.cat.6: Oversized IP packets sent to crash a target.
rb.cat.9: An open proxy, an open relay or a Tor exit node.
rb.cat.10: Comment or forum spam and other CMS spam.
rb.cat.11: Spam in the message body, infected attachments, phishing e-mails. Keep the comment to relevant facts.
rb.cat.12: Spam comments on blogs and CMS sites.
rb.cat.13: Combined category for addresses of VPN services.
rb.cat.14: Probing for open ports and vulnerable services.
rb.cat.17: Forging the identity of an e-mail sender.
rb.cat.18: Password guessing against websites and services (SSH, FTP, SIP, SMTP, RDP).
rb.cat.19: Scrapers and crawlers that ignore robots.txt or fake their user agent.
rb.cat.20: A host that is probably infected and used to attack others; combine with other categories.
rb.cat.21: Probing or exploiting web applications (CMS, shops, forums, plugins).
rb.cat.22: Abuse of Secure Shell; combine with a more specific category.
rb.cat.23: An attack aimed at an Internet-of-Things device; name the device type in the comment.
